headline: The deadlock ends here.
intro: You need experience to get hired. You need to be hired to get experience. That's the trap, and it's fake. Below are 20 real, self-contained jobs you can start right now, with no client and no permission. Each one produces a real deliverable: a reconciled set of books, a working automation, a finished video, a rebuilt calendar. Nobody asks whether you were paid for it. They ask whether you can do it. Now you can prove it.
creed: You don't need permission to do the work. No client, no problem, do the job anyway and the artifact IS your experience. Nobody asks whether you were paid for it; they ask whether you can do it. Nothing happens if you do nothing — start with one.

howItWorks.title: Prerequisite
howItWorks.desc: Know what you need before you start, and exactly where to get it free if you don't already have it.

howItWorks.title: Resources
howItWorks.desc: Real, specific, free resources, official docs, free courses, free tool tiers. No paid tools required for any task on this page.

howItWorks.title: The Task
howItWorks.desc: A realistic scenario, a concrete deliverable, real constraints, and numbered steps, the same shape of brief a real client would hand you.

howItWorks.title: Prove It
howItWorks.desc: What the finished artifact proves you can do, and exactly how to present it so it reads as evidence, not a school assignment.

tasks.title: Rescue a Founder's Inbox From Chaos
tasks.proves: You can build an inbox system that turns email chaos into a same-day response standard, the #1 thing founders hire executive ops for.

prerequisites.skill: Gmail labels, filters, and search operators
prerequisites.why: The whole triage system runs on labels + filters, if you can't nest labels or write a filter rule, you can't build the system.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Google's own Gmail Filters & Labels help center (free), 20 minutes, hands-on.

prerequisites.skill: A basic inbox triage decision framework (e.g. the 4 D's: Do, Delegate, Defer, Delete)
prerequisites.why: You need a decision rule for every email, not just folders to dump them in.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's /method, the UNSTICK and FIND methods teach the same decision-first thinking.

resources.name: Enron Email Dataset (Kaggle)
resources.what: A free, public, real corporate inbox (500k+ emails), pull a 50-email sample to stand in for your 'client's' inbox.

resources.name: Gmail Filters & Labels
resources.what: Official how-to for building the label taxonomy and auto-filters you'll design.

resources.name: Google Workspace Learning Center
resources.what: Fast primer on Gmail power-user features (search operators, multiple inboxes).

brief.scenario: Mara Dizon runs a 3-person SaaS startup solo. She hasn't opened her inbox in nine days, 400+ unread, real client requests buried under cold pitches and newsletters. She's about to miss a contract renewal because of it.
brief.deliverable: A 6-label triage taxonomy, a written triage SOP (the decision rule for every incoming email), and a worked example: 50 real emails from the Enron dataset sorted into your taxonomy with a one-line reason for each.
constraints: Maximum 6 labels, more than that isn't a system, it's a new mess.
Every label needs a plain-English rule for what goes in it.
Must include a stated response-time promise per label (e.g. 'Client, same business day').
steps: Download a 50–100 email sample from the Enron dataset.
Read all of them once, tallying what categories naturally emerge.
Design a 6-label taxonomy with a one-sentence rule per label.
Sort all 50 emails into your taxonomy, noting the reason for each call.
Write the triage SOP: how a new email gets labeled, when it gets answered, what gets auto-archived.
Write a 5-line 'inbox zero in 20 minutes' daily routine Mara can run herself.

definitionOfDone: Every one of the 50 sample emails has exactly one label.
Each label has a written rule a stranger could apply consistently.
The SOP names a response-time commitment for at least 3 of the labels.
A follow-up filter/search-operator query is written for at least 2 labels.
selfCritique: Could someone who's never met Mara sort her next 50 emails using only my SOP?
Did I create categories for how the emails actually clustered, or force them into a template?
Is any label vague enough that two people would file the same email differently?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a before/after: 'Inbox at 400+ unread, 9 days stale → sorted, labeled, SOP in place in 3 hours.' Screenshot the label sidebar and lead with the response-time promise, not the label names.
tasks.stretch: Build the actual Gmail filter rules (not just the taxonomy) using search operators, and write a 30-day audit checklist for keeping the inbox at zero.

tasks.title: Rebuild an Overbooked Executive's Calendar
tasks.proves: You can turn a reactive, back-to-back calendar into a protected, priority-driven schedule, the exact skill that gets you promoted to Chief of Staff.

prerequisites.skill: Google Calendar (recurring events, color-coding, multiple calendars)
prerequisites.why: The rebuild lives entirely in Calendar, you need to move fast in it.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Google Calendar Help Center's 'Get started' guide (free).

prerequisites.skill: Time-blocking and priority frameworks (Eisenhower matrix or similar)
prerequisites.why: You can't decide what to protect without a framework for what matters.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's Executive Operations track under /niches, or any free Eisenhower Matrix explainer.

resources.name: Google Calendar
resources.what: Build the actual before/after calendar mockup here (a free personal Google account works).

resources.name: Google Calendar Help Center
resources.what: Recurring events, working hours, and focus-time features you'll use in the rebuild.

resources.name: Eisenhower Matrix, free explainer
resources.what: The urgent/important framework you'll use to decide what gets protected first.

brief.scenario: Dan Reyes is regional director at a mid-size logistics company. His calendar has 11–14 meetings a day, back-to-back, zero focus time, and three standing meetings nobody can explain the purpose of anymore.
brief.deliverable: An audit scoring one invented sample week (you build it) against 5 red flags, plus a rebuilt version of that week in a real Google Calendar showing protected focus blocks, a meeting-free morning, and a trimmed recurring-meeting list.
constraints: The rebuilt week must include at least 2 protected 90-minute focus blocks.
At least 2 of the original recurring meetings must be cut, shortened, or converted to async.
Every kept meeting needs a one-line stated purpose.
steps: Construct the messy 'before' week: 12+ meetings across 5 days, mixed durations, no gaps (this is your practice raw material).
Audit it against 5 red flags: no purpose stated, no prep time, back-to-back with no buffer, recurring with unclear owner, wrong attendee count.
Decide which meetings to cut, shorten, delegate, or convert to async, write the reason for each.
Build the 'after' week in a real Google Calendar with color-coded categories and protected focus blocks.
Write a one-page 'calendar policy' Dan can hand to his team (buffer rules, no-meeting mornings, decline criteria).

definitionOfDone: Before and after week are both viewable (screenshots or shared calendar link).
Every cut or changed meeting has a documented reason.
The after week includes real protected focus time, not just fewer meetings.
The calendar policy doc is one page and usable by someone else.
selfCritique: Would Dan actually agree to every cut, or did I remove things without a real reason?
Did I protect focus time in the highest-energy part of the day, or just wherever there was a gap?
Is the policy doc specific enough to prevent the calendar from drifting back to chaos in a month?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the number: 'Cut a 14-meeting day to 8, added 3 hours of protected focus time per week.' Show the before/after calendar screenshots side by side.
tasks.stretch: Add a delegation matrix: for every cut meeting, name who could attend instead and draft the handoff message.

tasks.title: Reconcile Three Months of Messy Transactions
tasks.proves: You can take an unreconciled set of books and bring them current and audit-ready, the single skill that makes bookkeepers indispensable to a client.

prerequisites.skill: Double-entry bookkeeping basics (debits, credits, chart of accounts)
prerequisites.why: Reconciliation is meaningless if you don't understand what a transaction should hit.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Intuit's free QuickBooks Online Certification course covers this from zero.

prerequisites.skill: Bank reconciliation workflow inside QuickBooks Online or Xero
prerequisites.why: You need to actually run the reconciliation tool, not just understand the theory.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: QuickBooks Online's own free trial plus its in-app guided tour.

resources.name: QuickBooks Online Certification
resources.what: Official Intuit training, covers chart of accounts, reconciliation, and reporting.

resources.name: QuickBooks Online free trial
resources.what: 30-day free trial, do the actual reconciliation work inside the real tool, not a spreadsheet mockup.

resources.name: Kaggle sample bank transaction datasets
resources.what: Public sample transaction CSVs you can import as your practice client's messy bank feed.

brief.scenario: Riverside Coffee Roasters (a fictional 2-location café) hasn't reconciled its books since a bookkeeper quit three months ago. Owner transactions, duplicate vendor entries, and uncategorized deposits are piling up.
brief.deliverable: A QuickBooks Online (free trial) company file with 3 months of sample transactions imported, fully reconciled, chart of accounts cleaned up, and a one-page cleanup report documenting every issue you found and fixed.
constraints: Every transaction must be categorized, nothing left in 'Uncategorized.'
Any duplicate must be identified and flagged, not silently deleted.
The reconciliation must tie the ending bank balance to the statement balance exactly.
steps: Set up a free QuickBooks Online trial and create a practice company.
Import or manually enter ~60–100 sample transactions across 3 months (use a public sample dataset or build a realistic mix of sales, COGS, payroll, and owner draws).
Build/clean the chart of accounts to fit a small café business.
Categorize every transaction, flagging anything ambiguous.
Run the bank reconciliation for each of the 3 months until it ties out.
Write a cleanup report: what was wrong, what you fixed, what the owner should watch for going forward.

definitionOfDone: All 3 months show 'Reconciled' status with zero variance.
Zero transactions remain in an uncategorized or ask-my-accountant bucket.
The cleanup report lists at least 5 specific issues found and how each was resolved.
A basic P&L for the period can be generated without errors.
selfCritique: If the owner asked me to explain any single categorization, could I defend it?
Did I actually investigate ambiguous transactions, or guess and move on?
Does my cleanup report read like real findings, or like generic bookkeeping advice?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the before/after: '3 months, 0% reconciled → 100% reconciled, audit-ready in under a week.' Screenshot the reconciliation summary screen, it's the single most convincing proof in bookkeeping.
tasks.stretch: Add a recurring-transaction rule set (bank rules) that would auto-categorize 80% of future transactions without manual work.

tasks.title: Build an Accounts Receivable Aging Cleanup
tasks.proves: You can turn a wall of overdue invoices into a prioritized collection plan, the difference between a bookkeeper and a bookkeeper who actually protects cash flow.

prerequisites.skill: Accounts receivable basics (invoice, aging buckets, days sales outstanding)
prerequisites.why: You need to know what 30/60/90-day buckets mean before you can triage them.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Xero's free 'Accounts Receivable 101' help articles.

prerequisites.skill: Spreadsheet formulas (SUMIF, conditional formatting)
prerequisites.why: The aging report and prioritization live in a spreadsheet you build yourself.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's tracker-building lab at /build teaches the exact schema pattern you need.

resources.name: Xero Advisor Certification
resources.what: Covers AR workflows and aging reports inside Xero.

resources.name: Google Sheets
resources.what: Build the aging tracker and collection-priority sheet here.

resources.name: SCORE free templates library
resources.what: Reference real invoice/AR terminology used by small businesses (study only, don't copy).

brief.scenario: Bright Path Tutoring (a fictional small tutoring agency, 30 active family clients) has $18,400 in unpaid invoices, some over 90 days old, and no idea which ones are actually at risk of never getting paid.
brief.deliverable: An AR aging spreadsheet (30 invented but realistic invoices) with 30/60/90+ day buckets, a risk score per client, and a written collection plan with a specific message template for each aging bucket.
constraints: Every invoice needs an aging bucket calculated by formula, not typed in by hand.
The oldest 20% of balances must have an individual follow-up plan, not a generic template.
Collection messages must escalate in tone/urgency by bucket, 30-day and 90-day can't read the same.
steps: Build 30 realistic invoice records: client name, invoice date, amount, due date.
Add a formula-driven aging bucket column (Current / 30 / 60 / 90+).
Add conditional formatting so overdue severity is visible at a glance.
Calculate total dollars at risk per bucket and total days sales outstanding.
Write 3 escalating collection message templates (friendly reminder, firm follow-up, final notice).
Build a short collection plan prioritizing the highest-dollar, oldest-aging accounts first.

definitionOfDone: Aging buckets are 100% formula-driven, not manually assigned.
Total dollars at risk is calculated and correctly summed per bucket.
All 3 escalation message templates exist and are meaningfully different in tone.
The top 5 highest-risk accounts have a specific, individual next action noted.
selfCritique: If a client asked why I prioritized one overdue account over another, do I have a real reason?
Would the 90-day message actually get me paid, or does it read as passive as the 30-day one?
Did I build a formula that recalculates automatically if I change today's date?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the dollar figure: '$18,400 in receivables triaged into a prioritized 3-week collection plan.' Show the aging summary table as the hero visual, clients respond to the number.
tasks.stretch: Add a DSO (days sales outstanding) trend chart and a proposed late-payment policy (deposit requirements, interest terms) so the backlog doesn't recur.

tasks.title: Audit a Startup's Spending for Waste
tasks.proves: You can read raw expense data and surface real savings, proof you think like a financial partner, not just a data-entry clerk.

prerequisites.skill: Reading a P&L / expense report and recognizing common waste categories (duplicate subscriptions, unused seats, category creep)
prerequisites.why: The whole audit is pattern recognition across real spend categories.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's /method FIND drill, plus any free 'startup burn rate' explainer.

prerequisites.skill: Basic spreadsheet pivot tables or SUMIF grouping
prerequisites.why: You need to group and total expenses by vendor/category to spot the waste.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Google Sheets' own free pivot table tutorial in the Help Center.

resources.name: Google Sheets
resources.what: Build the expense audit and pivot summary here.

resources.name: Public SaaS spend benchmark reports
resources.what: Free published benchmarks on typical SaaS spend per employee, use to judge if a line item looks high.

resources.name: Public startup expense/burn breakdowns (Indie Hackers, r/SaaS threads)
resources.what: Real founders sharing real expense breakdowns, study the categories, not the numbers.

brief.scenario: Loopline (a fictional 12-person B2B SaaS startup) is burning faster than expected. The founder exports a year of expense data and asks: 'Where is this actually going, and what can we cut without hurting the team?'
brief.deliverable: A 12-month expense audit (build ~80 realistic line items yourself: software subscriptions, contractor payments, ads, travel) grouped by category, with the top 10 waste candidates flagged and a specific dollar-amount savings recommendation for each.
constraints: Every flagged item needs a stated reason (duplicate tool, unused seats, better alternative, wrong plan tier).
Recommendations must total to a specific annual savings number, not a vague estimate.
At least 3 flagged items must be software/SaaS spend, the most common startup leak.
steps: Build ~80 realistic expense line items across 12 months and 6–8 categories.
Group and total spend by category and by vendor using pivot tables.
Identify duplicate or overlapping tools (e.g. two project management apps).
Flag the top 10 waste candidates with a one-line reason each.
Calculate the total annual savings if all 10 recommendations were implemented.
Write a one-page summary memo for the founder, ranked by savings size.

definitionOfDone: Pivot table correctly totals spend by category and by vendor.
10 waste items are flagged, each with a specific dollar impact and reason.
Total savings figure is calculated, not estimated by eyeballing.
The memo is ranked biggest-savings-first, not in the order you found them.
selfCritique: Is every flagged item a real waste pattern, or did I pad the list to hit 10?
Would cutting my top recommendation actually hurt the team's ability to work?
Did I total the savings correctly, or is the headline number inflated?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the annual savings figure in bold: 'Found $14,200/year in recoverable spend across 10 line items.' The pivot table screenshot plus the ranked memo is the whole portfolio piece.
tasks.stretch: Add a spend policy, approval thresholds and a quarterly subscription-audit cadence, so the waste doesn't come back.

tasks.title: Audit a Real Public Brand's Social Presence
tasks.proves: You can diagnose why a brand's social isn't working using only public data, the exact research skill clients pay a social media manager to have.

prerequisites.skill: Reading engagement signals (likes/comments/shares relative to follower count, not absolute numbers)
prerequisites.why: A brand with 500k followers and 40 likes per post is doing worse than one with 5k followers and 300 likes, the ratio is what matters, not the raw count.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Meta's free Social Media Marketing course covers engagement-rate basics.

prerequisites.skill: Content calendar structure (pillars, cadence, format mix)
prerequisites.why: The audit ends in a calendar recommendation, you need the shape of one first.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's /build portfolio lab or Canva's free content calendar course.

resources.name: Meta Social Media Marketing
resources.what: Official Meta training on content strategy and engagement metrics.

resources.name: Any real public brand's Instagram/TikTok/LinkedIn (your choice)
resources.what: Your actual audit subject, no login needed, just their public posts from the last 30 days.

resources.name: Canva Design Essentials
resources.what: You'll need this to actually design the 3 finished posts for the deliverable.

brief.scenario: Pick one real, public local or regional brand (a café, gym, boutique, or small e-commerce shop) with an active but under-performing social account, you're auditing it cold, the way a prospective client would let you.
brief.deliverable: A written audit (posting cadence, format mix, engagement-rate calculation, tone consistency, bio/link-in-bio effectiveness) plus a 30-day content calendar and 3 fully finished posts (real graphics in Canva, real captions) that fix the biggest gap you found.
constraints: Audit must cover their last 15+ posts minimum, not a cherry-picked sample.
You must calculate an actual engagement rate, not describe it qualitatively.
The 3 finished posts must be publish-ready, full caption, hashtag set, and a real designed graphic.
steps: Choose a real, public brand's account and log their last 15–20 posts.
Calculate engagement rate per post and average it; note posting cadence and format mix (photo/video/carousel).
Identify the single biggest gap (inconsistent posting, weak captions, no video, unclear bio, no CTA).
Design a 30-day content calendar with 3 content pillars addressing that gap.
Design and write 3 fully finished posts in Canva that demonstrate the fix.
Write a one-page audit summary a business owner could read in 3 minutes.

definitionOfDone: Engagement rate is calculated with a shown formula, not just stated as a number.
The single biggest gap is named specifically, backed by evidence from the post data.
30-day calendar has clear pillars and a stated cadence (e.g. 4x/week).
All 3 finished posts are complete, graphic, caption, hashtags, ready to publish.
selfCritique: Would this brand's actual owner recognize the gap I identified as their real problem?
Do my 3 sample posts sound like this brand's voice, or like generic social media copy?
Did I calculate engagement rate correctly (engagement ÷ followers, not ÷ posts)?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a case study: brand name, before engagement rate, the gap you found, and your 3 finished posts as visual proof. Never claim you worked for the brand, label it clearly as an unsolicited audit/practice project.
tasks.stretch: Turn the audit into a cold outreach message pitching the brand owner directly, using the application-message lab's 4-part structure.

tasks.title: Build a Repeatable 30-Day Content Calendar System
tasks.proves: You can design a content system that survives past day one, pillars, cadence, and a repeatable production process, not just a list of post ideas.

prerequisites.skill: Content pillar strategy (3–5 recurring themes that support a brand's goals)
prerequisites.why: A calendar without pillars is just a list of random ideas that runs out in two weeks.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: HubSpot's free content strategy course covers pillar-based planning.

prerequisites.skill: Spreadsheet-based tracker design
prerequisites.why: The calendar itself is a tracker, status, dates, and an owner column.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's /build 'Build Your Own Tracker' lab teaches the exact schema.

resources.name: HubSpot Content Marketing Certification
resources.what: Covers pillar strategy, cadence planning, and repurposing content across formats.

resources.name: Google Sheets
resources.what: Build the actual 30-day calendar tracker here, status column, dates, format, caption draft.

resources.name: Buffer's free content calendar guide
resources.what: Real-world cadence benchmarks by platform (how often to post on IG vs TikTok vs LinkedIn).

brief.scenario: Coastal Grind (a fictional independent coffee roastery, one location, growing wholesale side) wants a consistent social presence but has posted only 4 times in the last 2 months, with no plan.
brief.deliverable: A 30-day content calendar spreadsheet with 4 content pillars, a stated posting cadence per platform, and every single day's post pre-planned with format, hook idea, and caption draft, plus 3 of those days fully designed and written as finished posts.
constraints: Exactly 4 content pillars, each tied to a specific business goal (e.g. wholesale leads, in-store foot traffic, brand story, product education).
Every calendar row needs a format (photo/video/carousel/reel), not just a topic.
The tracker must have a status column (Idea / Drafted / Scheduled / Posted) using data validation, per the tracker-lab pattern.
steps: Define 4 content pillars mapped to Coastal Grind's actual business goals.
Build the 30-day calendar spreadsheet: date, pillar, format, hook, caption draft, status.
Fill in all 30 days with real, specific ideas, no placeholder 'post something' rows.
Apply data validation to the status column and conditional formatting for overdue/unposted days.
Fully design and write 3 representative days as finished, publish-ready posts.
Write a short 'how to keep this alive' note: who updates it, how often, what happens when an idea runs dry.

definitionOfDone: All 30 days are filled with distinct, specific content ideas, no repeats, no filler.
Every pillar appears roughly evenly across the 30 days, not lopsided.
Status column uses a real dropdown (data validation), not free text.
3 finished posts exist as real deliverables, not just calendar rows.
selfCritique: If I deleted the pillar labels, could someone still tell which pillar each post belongs to?
Is this calendar something a real business could actually execute, or is it aspirational fluff?
Did I vary the format enough, or is it 30 days of static photos?
tasks.presentIt: Show the full calendar as a scrollable screenshot alongside the 3 finished posts. Lead with the system, not the ideas: 'Built a 30-day content engine with 4 pillars and a self-sustaining production tracker.'
tasks.stretch: Add a repurposing map showing how each pillar's content can be cut into 3 different formats (a Reel becomes a carousel becomes a caption-only post) to triple output without new ideas.

tasks.title: Produce a 3-Part Short-Form Video Series for a Public Product
tasks.proves: You can plan, shoot, and edit short-form video that follows a proven hook-retention-CTA structure, the highest-leverage, highest-pay skill in social media right now.

prerequisites.skill: Short-form video structure (hook in first 2 seconds, retention pacing, clear CTA)
prerequisites.why: Random footage with music isn't a strategy, the structure is what makes it convert.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's CapCut Editing Masterclass under the Social Media track, or CapCut's own free tutorials.

prerequisites.skill: Basic phone-shot video (framing, lighting, stable shots) and CapCut editing
prerequisites.why: You're producing real finished video, not a storyboard, you need the actual production skill.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: CapCut's in-app tutorials (free) walk through cuts, captions, and pacing.

resources.name: CapCut
resources.what: Free mobile/desktop editor, shoot and edit all 3 videos here.

resources.name: TikTok Creative Center (public, free)
resources.what: Real published top-performing ad and organic examples by category, study structure, don't copy content.

resources.name: CapCut Editing Masterclass
resources.what: DevUp's own walkthrough of short-form editing fundamentals.

brief.scenario: You're building a UGC-style (user-generated-content style) video series for a real product you personally own or can access for free (a phone app, a drugstore skincare item, a snack, a public library service), treat it like a real brand deal even though nobody asked you to.
brief.deliverable: 3 finished short-form videos (15–45 seconds each, vertical, captioned) following a hook → problem → demo → CTA structure, each targeting a different angle on the same product (e.g. a pain-point angle, a comparison angle, a 'day in the life' angle).
constraints: Each video must hook within the first 2 seconds, no slow intros.
All 3 videos must have burned-in captions (accessibility + muted-autoplay reality).
Each video needs a distinct angle, 3 versions of the same script don't count.
steps: Pick a real, accessible product and study 5 real public examples of similar UGC-style content for structure.
Write 3 short scripts, each with a different angle, using a hook/problem/demo/CTA outline.
Shoot raw footage for all 3 (phone camera is fine, natural light, stable frame).
Edit each in CapCut: cuts on beat, captions burned in, background audio at appropriate level.
Export all 3 in vertical 9:16 format, ready to publish.
Write a one-line strategic rationale for each video's angle.

definitionOfDone: All 3 videos are fully edited, captioned, and exported, not scripts or storyboards.
Each hooks within 2 seconds (test by watching only the first 2 seconds, does it make sense to keep watching?).
Captions are accurate and burned in, not relying on platform auto-captions.
Each video has a clearly different angle from the other two.
selfCritique: Would I stop scrolling in the first 2 seconds if this appeared in my own feed?
Is the CTA clear, or does the video just end?
Do the 3 videos actually feel different, or are they the same video with different words?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a mini case study: the product, the 3 angles chosen and why, the videos, and what you'd test next (a 4th angle, a different hook style). This is the single strongest portfolio piece for a video-focused social role.
tasks.stretch: Post all 3 publicly on a real account and track actual view/engagement data for 7 days, real performance data beats any mockup.

tasks.title: Rescue a Chaotic Agency Sprint Board
tasks.proves: You can take an unmanaged task list and turn it into a board that actually tells the team what to do next, the core job of a PM.

prerequisites.skill: Kanban/sprint basics (backlog, in-progress, review, done; WIP limits)
prerequisites.why: Without a structure, you're just moving cards around, not managing a sprint.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Asana Academy's free 'Kanban fundamentals' course.

prerequisites.skill: Writing a task/user story that a stranger could execute without asking questions
prerequisites.why: A board full of vague tasks ('fix the thing') is unmanageable no matter how it's organized.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's SOP-building lab at /build teaches the same one-action-per-step discipline.

resources.name: Asana Academy
resources.what: Official Asana training on sprint boards, dependencies, and workload views.

resources.name: Asana / ClickUp / Trello free tier
resources.what: Build the actual rescued board here (any of the three has a generous free plan).

resources.name: Google Project Management Certificate (audit free)
resources.what: Coursera lets you audit the full course free, covers sprint planning and risk tracking.

brief.scenario: Halden Creative (a fictional 8-person design agency) runs client work through one giant unsorted task list, 60+ tasks, no owners on a third of them, no due dates, three tasks marked 'urgent' that have sat for a month.
brief.deliverable: A rebuilt sprint board (in Asana, ClickUp, or Trello free tier) with 60 realistic tasks organized into a proper Kanban structure, clear columns, WIP limits, every task with an owner, due date, and client tag, plus a one-page 'how we run sprints now' SOP.
constraints: Every task must have an owner and a due date, no exceptions, even placeholder tasks.
WIP limit on the 'In Progress' column, enforced and explained.
At least 10 of the original 60 tasks must be identified as duplicates, stale, or no longer needed and explicitly archived (not silently deleted).
steps: Build the messy 'before' state: 60 realistic agency tasks across 4 client projects, deliberately disorganized (this is your practice raw material).
Audit the list: flag duplicates, stale tasks, and missing owners/dates.
Design the board structure: columns, WIP limits, tagging system by client.
Migrate and clean all 60 tasks into the new board with full metadata.
Archive (don't delete) the flagged duplicates/stale items with a note on why.
Write the one-page sprint SOP: how a task enters the board, how WIP limits are enforced, what 'done' means.

definitionOfDone: 100% of tasks on the new board have an owner and a due date.
WIP limit is set and would visibly block overloading a column.
At least 10 stale/duplicate tasks were found, archived, and logged with a reason.
The SOP defines a clear Definition of Done for at least one task type.
selfCritique: Could a new hire look at this board and know exactly what to work on next?
Did I actually reduce chaos, or just make the same chaos look tidier?
Is my WIP limit realistic for an 8-person team, or arbitrary?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the before/after count: '60 unsorted tasks, 1/3 with no owner → fully triaged sprint board with WIP limits and a working SOP.' Screenshot both board states side by side.
tasks.stretch: Add a workload view showing each team member's current load, and flag anyone over-allocated relative to the others.

tasks.title: Build a Cross-Team Status Reporting Dashboard
tasks.proves: You can turn scattered project updates into a single dashboard leadership can read in 60 seconds, the artifact that gets PMs trusted with bigger scope.

prerequisites.skill: RAG (Red/Amber/Green) status reporting and risk tracking
prerequisites.why: A dashboard without a clear status logic is just a pretty spreadsheet.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Google's free Project Management Certificate module on stakeholder reporting.

steps: Build 5 invented project workstreams, each with 10–15 underlying tasks with due dates and completion status.
Define the RAG logic explicitly (e.g. Red = any milestone overdue by 5+ days, Amber = at risk, Green = on track).
Build formulas that calculate each project's status automatically from the task data.

tasks.title: Build a Support Macro & Response Library
tasks.proves: You can turn repetitive support questions into fast, on-brand, still-human responses, the skill that lets a support team handle 3x the volume without feeling robotic.

prerequisites.skill: Customer support tone (empathetic but efficient, not scripted-sounding)
prerequisites.why: A macro that reads like a robot defeats the purpose, the client's brand voice has to survive templating.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: HubSpot's free Service Hub course covers tone and macro design.

prerequisites.skill: Common support ticket categorization (billing, technical, general/how-to, complaint)
prerequisites.why: You can't build useful macros without knowing what the recurring ticket types actually are.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Zendesk's free help-center articles on ticket categorization.

resources.name: HubSpot Service Hub
resources.what: Covers support workflows, macros, and tone-of-voice guidelines.

resources.name: A real free SaaS tool's public help center (your choice)
resources.what: Study their actual support-facing language and common questions, this is material to study, not copy.

resources.name: Google Docs
resources.what: Build the actual macro library here, organized and ready to hand to a support team.

brief.scenario: Pixelroom (a fictional design-tool SaaS, ~2,000 users) has one support person answering the same 15 questions over and over, writing every reply from scratch, with response times creeping past 24 hours.
brief.deliverable: A 15-macro support library covering the 4 most common ticket categories (billing, technical, how-to, complaint/refund), each macro with a merge-field placeholder for personalization, plus a one-page usage guide on when to use which macro and how to keep replies from sounding canned.
constraints: Every macro must include at least one merge-field placeholder (e.g. {{customer_name}}, {{plan_type}}), no fully generic replies.
At least 3 macros must handle a difficult scenario (refund denial, angry customer, bug with no fix ETA), not just easy how-to questions.
Each macro capped at 120 words, support replies that ramble don't get read.
steps: Research a real SaaS product's public help docs to identify realistic recurring question types.
List the 15 most common ticket types across the 4 categories.
Draft each macro with merge fields, staying under 120 words and matching a warm-but-efficient tone.
Write 3 'hard mode' macros for genuinely difficult scenarios (angry customer, denied refund, no ETA).
Write the usage guide: when to send as-is vs. when to personalize further, and a rule against pasting into an emotionally escalated conversation without editing.

definitionOfDone: All 15 macros are written, categorized, and under the 120-word cap.
Every macro has at least one merge field.
3 macros specifically address a hard/emotional scenario, not just routine FAQs.
The usage guide states a clear rule for when NOT to use a macro unedited.
selfCritique: If I received this reply as a frustrated customer, would it feel human or robotic?
Does the refund-denial macro actually de-escalate, or does it sound defensive?
Are the merge fields realistic, data a support agent would actually have on hand?
tasks.presentIt: Present the library as a formatted doc with categories clearly labeled. Lead with the practical value: '15 macros covering 80% of recurring tickets, cutting average reply-drafting time from 5 minutes to 30 seconds.'
tasks.stretch: Add a tiered escalation macro set, first reply, follow-up after 48 hours of silence, and final notice, for tickets that go quiet mid-conversation.

prerequisites.ifYouDont: Any free tool works, Windows Snipping Tool, macOS Preview, or Canva's free annotation features.

resources.name: Zendesk Support
resources.what: Covers knowledge-base structure and self-service support best practices.

resources.name: Notion (free tier)
resources.what: Build and publish the article set here, real formatting, real inline images.

brief.scenario: Pick one real, free-tier SaaS tool with a feature you (or people in its public community/support forums) find genuinely confusing, e.g. a permissions system, an export/import flow, a pricing-tier limit that's unclear. This is real friction, not invented.
brief.deliverable: A 3-article knowledge-base set (a getting-started article, a troubleshooting/FAQ article, and an advanced-use-case article) covering that one confusing feature end to end, with annotated screenshots, written in the tool's actual voice/terminology.
constraints: All 3 articles must reference the actual current UI of the tool (test it live, don't guess from memory).
At least 6 annotated screenshots total across the set.
The troubleshooting article must address at least 3 real confusion points you can point to (from your own use or public forum threads).
steps: Use the tool's free tier yourself and find where you (or the public forums) get stuck on this feature.
Outline the 3-article structure: getting-started, troubleshooting/FAQ, advanced use case.
Walk through the feature step by step, screenshotting every meaningful UI state.
Write the getting-started article with numbered, one-action steps.
Write the troubleshooting article addressing the specific confusion points you found.
Write the advanced article for a power-user scenario, and annotate all screenshots.

definitionOfDone: All 3 articles are complete, formatted, and published in a real doc tool (Notion or similar).
Every step-heavy section has a supporting annotated screenshot.
The troubleshooting article names real, specific confusion points, not a generic 'having trouble? contact support.'
Terminology matches the tool's actual UI exactly (no invented button names).
selfCritique: Could someone who's never opened this feature complete it using only my getting-started article?
Did my troubleshooting article solve real friction, or restate the obvious?
Would the tool's own support team find this useful enough to actually publish?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a labeled case study: the tool, the specific feature, the friction point, and the 3 articles (link to the published Notion pages). Note explicitly this was unsolicited practice work, not commissioned by the company.
tasks.stretch: Send the article set as a genuinely helpful, no-strings message to the tool's support or community team, some companies do publish community-contributed docs.

brief.scenario: Agent Priya Nair has a listing that's been on the market 45 days with 12 showings and zero offers. Her feedback is scattered across texts, emails, and memory, she can't tell if it's a price problem or a staging problem.
brief.deliverable: A showing feedback tracker (12 realistic showing entries) with structured feedback categories (price, condition, layout, location, staging), a scored summary showing which factor is mentioned most, and a one-page recommendation memo (price cut vs. staging fix vs. hold) backed by the data.
constraints: Every showing entry needs a structured feedback category via dropdown, not free-text only.
The tracker must calculate which factor was flagged most often, by formula.
The recommendation memo must cite the actual data (e.g. '7 of 12 showings flagged price'), not just an opinion.
steps: Research a real comparable public listing for realistic price/detail reference.
Build 12 realistic showing feedback entries: date, agent, structured category, free-text detail, interest level.
Add data validation dropdowns for the feedback category and interest level.
Build a formula-driven summary counting mentions per category.
Analyze the summary to identify the dominant issue.
Write a one-page recommendation memo to Priya citing the specific data behind your recommendation.

definitionOfDone: All 12 entries are logged with a structured (dropdown) category, not free text alone.
The summary count is formula-driven and updates if a new entry is added.
The memo's recommendation directly cites the tracker's data (a specific count or percentage).

selfCritique: Does my recommendation follow logically from the data, or did I decide first and cherry-pick support?
Would Priya be able to act on this memo immediately, or does it need more explanation?
Is the tracker something she could keep using for her next listing without me?

tasks.stretch: Extend the tracker to auto-flag any listing with 10+ showings and zero offers as needing a review, so it becomes a system Priya reuses across her whole pipeline, not a one-off.

constraints: Sequence must be segmented, hot leads get faster/more touches than cold leads, explicitly.
Every touch needs real, finished copy, no placeholder text.
The tracker must show current sequence position per lead, using the ID/status/date-trigger schema pattern.
steps: Define 3 lead temperature tiers and the criteria for each (e.g. hot = requested a showing, warm = engaged with content, cold = no response yet).
Design the touch cadence per tier (e.g. hot: day 0, 1, 3, 7; cold: day 0, 5, 15, 30).
Write real copy for all touches, a mix of text, email, and a call-prompt/script.
Build 15 realistic sample leads with names, source, and current temperature.
Build the tracker showing each lead's current position in their sequence and next scheduled touch.
Write a short SOP: how a lead gets classified, and what happens when a lead goes silent past the last touch.

definitionOfDone: All touches across all 3 tiers have complete, non-placeholder copy.
The cadence is visibly different by tier (hot leads touched more, faster).
Tracker shows a specific next-action date per lead, calculated from their entry date.
The SOP defines what happens after the final touch with no response.
selfCritique: Would I personally feel nurtured or harassed if I received this exact sequence as a lead?
Is the hot-lead cadence actually faster, or did I just relabel the same timing?
Does the tracker tell Marcus exactly who to contact today without him doing any thinking?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the scale and the system: '40 stalled leads → a 12-touch, temperature-segmented follow-up system with full message copy and a live tracker.' Show one hot and one cold sequence side by side to prove the differentiation.
tasks.stretch: Add a re-engagement 'break-up' message for leads that go fully silent past day 45, the last touch designed to get either a yes or a clean no.

resources.what: Vendor-provided course covering trigger/action design and common patterns.

brief.scenario: Northline Consulting (a fictional 4-person consultancy) collects new-client inquiries through a website contact form, then someone manually copy-pastes each one into a tracking spreadsheet, inconsistently, with a 2-day average lag and occasional lost leads.
brief.deliverable: A real, working Zapier (or Make) automation connecting a Google Form to a Google Sheets CRM-style tracker, auto-populating a new row with a unique ID, timestamp, and status on every form submission, plus a written SOP explaining the automation for a non-technical team to trust and maintain it.
constraints: The automation must be live and tested with at least 3 real test submissions, not just configured and untested.
Every new row must auto-generate a unique lead ID and default status (per the tracker-lab schema pattern).

steps: Build the intake form (Google Forms) with the fields a real consulting inquiry needs.
Build the destination tracker (Google Sheets) using the tracker-lab schema: unique ID, status dropdown, date trigger, notes.
Build the Zap/scenario: trigger on form submission, action creates a new sheet row.
Configure auto-generated fields (ID, timestamp, default status) inside the automation.
Test with 3 real submissions and verify data lands correctly every time.
Write the SOP: how it works, how to check if it's broken, and the manual fallback steps.

definitionOfDone: The Zap/scenario is live (not just built in draft) and successfully tested with 3+ real submissions.
Every new row includes a correctly auto-generated unique ID and default status.
The SOP includes a specific manual fallback process for automation failure.
No manual copy-paste step remains in the described workflow.
selfCritique: Did I actually test this with real submissions, or just trust the configuration screen?
If the Zap silently failed for a week, would anyone notice, and does my SOP address that?
Would a non-technical team member trust and be able to explain this system to a client?
tasks.presentIt: Show the automation diagram (trigger → action) plus a screenshot of a real test submission landing correctly in the sheet. Lead with the time saved: 'Eliminated a 2-day manual entry lag and its lost-lead risk with one automated Zap.'
tasks.stretch: Add a second automated step: an auto-confirmation email to the lead and a Slack/email notification to the team the moment a new inquiry arrives.

brief.scenario: Solstice Design Co (a fictional 3-person freelance design collective) tracks clients, projects, and invoices across 3 disconnected spreadsheets that constantly go out of sync, a client's name gets updated in one and not the other two.

constraints: Tables must be genuinely linked (Airtable link fields), not just similarly-named columns across separate flat tables.

steps: Design the schema: 3 tables, their fields, and how they link to each other.
Build the Contacts table with realistic sample data (10+ contacts).
Build the Projects table, linked to Contacts, with a status field and at least one rollup/lookup from Contacts.
Build the Invoices table, linked to Projects, with amount, due date, and paid-status fields.
Build a kanban view by project status and a filtered view for overdue invoices.
Build and test one real automation (e.g. status-change notification).

definitionOfDone: All 3 tables are populated with realistic linked sample data (10+ records each).
At least one lookup/rollup field correctly pulls linked data across tables.
Both required views (kanban by status, filtered overdue invoices) exist and work correctly.
The automation has been triggered and tested at least once, with proof (screenshot/log).
selfCritique: If I updated a contact's name once, does it correctly reflect everywhere it's referenced?
Would a real freelancer actually replace their 3 spreadsheets with this, or is something missing?
Is my schema over-built with fields nobody would actually use, or genuinely lean?

Write and iterate a classification prompt that returns a fixed-category output reliably.
Build the automation: form/trigger → AI classification step → routing action into a tracker.
Run all 15 test tickets through the live automation.

Write a short 'known limitations' note, where a human should still double-check the AI's call.

The AI step returns one of the fixed categories consistently, not inconsistent free text.
An honest accuracy report exists, including at least one real misclassification, analyzed.

selfCritique: Did I report the real accuracy, including failures, or only show my best runs?

prerequisites.ifYouDont: Canva Design Essentials (free).

resources.name: Canva Design Essentials
resources.what: Covers compositing, text hierarchy, and export settings for thumbnail-sized images.

resources.name: A real public YouTube channel in a niche you like (your choice)
resources.what: Study their actual published video titles/thumbnails for the real subject matter you'll design for.

resources.name: TubeBuddy or vidIQ free tier
resources.what: Free thumbnail-preview simulators show how your design looks at actual small sizes across devices.

brief.scenario: Pick one real, public video (yours if you have one, or a real public video you'd redesign as a practice exercise, never claim you made the actual video) and design 3 genuinely different thumbnail concepts testing 3 different psychological hooks (curiosity gap, big-number/stat callout, emotional face reaction).
brief.deliverable: 3 finished, export-ready thumbnail designs (1280x720) for the same video, each built around a distinct hook strategy, plus a written A/B test hypothesis for each ('I expect Concept B to outperform because...') and a small-size readability check screenshot for all 3.
constraints: All 3 thumbnails must be for the exact same video/topic, variation must come from strategy, not from designing 3 different videos.
Each thumbnail needs 5 words of text or fewer, YouTube's own design guidance, not a suggestion.
You must screenshot all 3 at simulated small size (like a mobile home feed) to prove readability.
steps: Choose a real public video/topic to redesign as practice.
Define 3 distinct hook strategies (curiosity gap, stat/number callout, emotional reaction).
Design thumbnail concept 1 at full 1280x720 resolution.
Design thumbnail concept 2 and concept 3, each genuinely different in composition, not just recolored.
Shrink all 3 down to simulate a mobile feed and screenshot the readability test.
Write a one-line testable hypothesis for each concept explaining why it might win.

definitionOfDone: All 3 thumbnails are exported at correct 1280x720 resolution.
Each uses a genuinely different composition/hook, not a palette-swap of the same layout.
Text is 5 words or fewer on every thumbnail.
All 3 pass the small-size readability check (legible and clear at simulated mobile size).
selfCritique: If I saw all 3 in a crowded YouTube feed at actual size, could I read the text and understand the hook in under 1 second?
Are the 3 concepts testing genuinely different hooks, or minor variations of the same idea?
Would my hypothesis for the 'winning' concept actually be falsifiable by real click-through data?
tasks.presentIt: Present all 3 side by side at both full size and simulated small size, with the hypothesis for each labeled clearly. Frame it as an A/B test plan, not just 'here are 3 thumbnails', the testing methodology is the actual skill being proven.
tasks.stretch: If you have access to a real channel (yours or with permission), actually run the test live and report real click-through-rate data after a few days.

tasks.title: Edit a 60-Second Product Explainer From Raw Screen Recordings
tasks.proves: You can turn raw, unscripted screen-recording footage into a tight, professional explainer video, a deliverable SaaS and app companies pay well for on a recurring basis.

prerequisites.skill: Screen recording basics (a free tool like OBS Studio or a built-in OS recorder)
prerequisites.why: You need real raw footage to edit, this task isn't about stock footage, it's about turning messy screen capture into something polished.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: OBS Studio's own free getting-started guide, or your OS's built-in screen recorder (no install needed).

prerequisites.skill: Video editing fundamentals: cuts, pacing, text overlays, background music licensing
prerequisites.why: The explainer needs professional pacing and legally clean audio, not just raw footage with a voiceover.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's CapCut Editing Masterclass, or CapCut/DaVinci Resolve's own free tutorials.

resources.name: OBS Studio (free, open source)
resources.what: Record raw screen footage of the free tool you'll be explaining.

resources.name: CapCut or DaVinci Resolve (free tier)
resources.what: Edit the final explainer here, both have generous free tiers sufficient for a 60-second video.

resources.name: YouTube Audio Library (free, royalty-free music)
resources.what: Legally clean background music, never use unlicensed commercial tracks in client-style work.

brief.scenario: Pick one real, free-tier SaaS or app tool you genuinely use or can access (a note app, a free design tool, a habit tracker) and treat it as a client who needs a 60-second 'what is this and why should I care' explainer for their landing page.
brief.deliverable: A finished 60-second explainer video: raw screen recording of the tool's core feature, edited with a clear 3-act structure (problem → solution demo → CTA), text overlays for key points, licensed background music, and a written voiceover script (recorded yourself, or as on-screen text if you're not comfortable on mic).
constraints: Must be 60 seconds or under, explainer videos live or die on tightness, not completeness.
Must follow a problem → solution → CTA structure, explicitly identifiable in the edit.
Background music must be from a verifiably free/licensed source, no exceptions.
steps: Choose a real free tool and identify its single clearest core value proposition.
Write a tight script: what problem it solves (10–15 sec), how it works (30–35 sec), CTA (10–15 sec).
Record raw screen footage demonstrating the actual product flow, cleanly and deliberately.
Edit: cut down to the essential moments, add text overlays for key points, sync pacing to the script.
Add licensed background music at an appropriately low volume under any voiceover.
Export at a standard resolution (1080p) and do a final full watch-through for pacing issues.

definitionOfDone: Final video is 60 seconds or under, exported and playable.
The problem → solution → CTA structure is clearly identifiable when watching.
All footage is real screen recording of the actual tool, not stock footage or slides.
Music is confirmed royalty-free/licensed, and audio levels don't drown out any voiceover or overlay text.
selfCritique: Would someone unfamiliar with this tool understand what it does and why they'd want it after watching once?
Did I cut every dead moment, or does the pacing drag anywhere?
Is the CTA clear and specific, or does the video just fade out?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a mini case study: the tool, the core value prop you chose to lead with, and the finished video embedded/linked. Lead with the constraint you nailed: 'Turned raw, unscripted screen capture into a 58-second, problem-solution-CTA explainer.'
tasks.stretch: Cut a second, 15-second vertical version of the same explainer for social/story placements, proving you can adapt one asset across formats, a real recurring client need.

tasks.title: Deliver One Pro-Bono Project for a Real Organization
tasks.time: 1–2 weeks, a few hours per week
tasks.proves: You can scope, deliver, and hand over real work for a real stakeholder — with a named organization willing to vouch for it. This is the closest thing to client experience that requires no client.

prerequisites.skill: One deliverable you can already produce (from any other task on this page)
prerequisites.why: Pro-bono work is where you apply a skill for a real stakeholder, not where you learn it from zero. Bring one thing you can do.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Finish one Starter micro-task above first — it gives you the exact deliverable to offer.

resources.name: Your own community
resources.what: A school, parish, barangay health center, co-op, or small local business — every one of them has a broken spreadsheet, an unmanaged page, or books nobody reconciles.

brief.scenario: Choose one real organization near you and offer one clearly-scoped piece of work, free. Choose where your hours do the most good — a small org with no budget gains more from ten of your hours than a large one ever would, and effective help is targeted: one real problem, solved completely, handed over so they can keep it running without you.
brief.deliverable: The finished work itself, plus a one-page handover the org can use after you leave: what you built, how to maintain it, and where everything lives.
constraints: Scope it in writing before you start — one deliverable, one deadline, agreed with a named person. Pro-bono without scope becomes an unpaid job.
Treat it exactly like paid work: professional communication, deadlines kept, confidentiality respected. This is conduct practice as much as craft practice.
Deliver a handover document. Work that collapses when you leave helped nobody.
steps: List 3 organizations you already have a connection to, and for each, one visible problem you could fix.
Contact the most promising one with a specific offer: the problem, the deliverable, the deadline. Specific offers get yes; vague offers get silence.
Agree the scope in writing (a message thread counts). Then deliver it like a paid engagement.
Hand over: walk them through the work, leave the one-page guide, and ask one question — 'may I show this work, with your name, when I apply for jobs?'

definitionOfDone: The deliverable is live and in use by the organization, not just finished on your laptop.
A named person at the org has the handover document and can run things without you.
You have written permission to present the work publicly.
selfCritique: Did I scope this in writing before starting, or did the work grow past the agreement?
Could the org keep using what I built if I disappeared today?
Did I pick the org where my hours did the most good, or just the easiest ask?
tasks.presentIt: Present it as your first case study: the organization, the problem, the deliverable, and one real outcome. 'Rebuilt the enrollment sheet for a 40-student tutorial center; staff now update it themselves' beats any certificate on the page.
tasks.stretch: After handover, offer a second org the same deliverable. Two named organizations plus two handover docs is a portfolio — and a referral network you earned by giving first.
